Solution. Answer: 48. Call the perimeter of one of the four congruent parts $p$. Then $p$ is made up of a quarter-circle of radius 32 cm and two semicircles of radius 16 cm , i.e.
$$ \begin{aligned} p & =\frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 \pi \cdot 32+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \pi \cdot 16 \\ & =16 \pi+32 \pi \\ & =48 \pi \mathrm{~cm} \\ \therefore x & =48 \end{aligned} $$

wajo25_q2.solution:
Solution. Answer: 487. Since 973 is positive, $a$ must be the larger integer.
$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore b & =a-1 \\ \therefore 973 & =a^{2}-b^{2} \\ & =(a+b)(a-b) \\ & =(a+b) \cdot 1 \\ & =a+a-1 \\ \therefore 974 & =2 a \\ a & =487 . \end{aligned} $$
Alternative 1. Since $a$ must be larger, $b=a-1$. So,
$$ \begin{aligned} 973 & =a^{2}-(a-1)^{2} \\ & =2 a-1 \\ \therefore 974 & =2 a \\ a & =487 . \end{aligned} $$
Alternative 2. Working with $b$ which must be the smaller (fewer minus signs), $a=b+1$.
$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore 973 & =(b+1)^{2}-b^{2} \\ & =2 b+1 \\ \therefore 972 & =2 b \\ b & =486 \\ a & =b+1 \\ & =487 . \end{aligned} $$

wajo25_q3.solution:
Solution. Answer: 400. "No hat" can be counted as a $4^{\text {th }}$ hat, and "no runners" can be counted as a $5^{\text {th }}$ pair of runners. Thus the number of outfit combinations (and hence the number of days to try them all out) is:
"no. of T-shirts" $\cdot$ "no. of shorts" $\cdot$ "no. of hats" $\cdot$ "no. of runners"
$$ \begin{aligned} & =5 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \\ & =400 \end{aligned} $$
Note. Without counting "no hat" as a $4^{\text {th }}$ hat, and "no runners" as a $5^{\text {th }}$ pair of runners, we would have 4 cases to count separately. Below we show the equivalence of the approaches.
$$ \begin{aligned} 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 5= & 5 \cdot 4 \cdot(3+1) \cdot(4+1) \\ = & 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 4+ \\ & 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 1+ \\ & 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 4+ \\ & 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \end{aligned} $$
The three last lines are the counts for: "no runners", "no hat" and "no hat and no runners", respectively.

wajo25_q7.solution:
Solution. Answer: 168. The interior angle sum of an $n$-gon is $(n-2) 180^{\circ}$.
So each angle of a regular 5-gon is $3 \cdot 180 / 5=108^{\circ}$.
$$ \begin{aligned} \angle A E F & =\angle A E D-\angle F E D \\ & =108^{\circ}-60^{\circ} \\ & =48^{\circ} \\ \therefore \angle A F E & =\frac{1}{2}\left(180^{\circ}-\angle A E F\right), \text { since } \triangle A E F \text { isos. } \\ & =\angle C F D, \text { by symmetry } \\ \therefore \angle A F C & =360^{\circ}-(\angle A F E+\angle C F D+\angle E F D) \\ & =360^{\circ}-\left(180^{\circ}-48^{\circ}+60^{\circ}\right) \\ & =168^{\circ} \end{aligned} $$

wajo25_q9.solution:
Solution. Answer: 19. Observe that the sum $S$ of the numbers on the board is a monovariant; that is, $S$ reduces by 1000 each turn.
Furthermore, each turn reduces the number of numbers by exactly 1.
So it will take 2024 "moves" for the game to halt.
Thus, the final number on the board must be,
$$ \begin{aligned} (1+2+3+\cdots+2025)-1000 \cdot 2024 & =\frac{(1+2025)}{2} \cdot 2025-1000 \cdot 2024 \\ & =1013 \cdot 2025-1000 \cdot 2024 \\ & =1000 \cdot(2025-2024)+13 \cdot 2025 \\ & =1000+26325 \\ & =27325 \end{aligned} $$
which has digit sum $2+7+3+2+5=19$.

wajo25_q10.solution:
Solution. Answer: 192. Let the required positive integer be $N$ and suppose
$$N=p_{1}^{e_{1}} p_{2}^{e_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{e_{k}}$$
is its prime decomposition, where $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{k}$ are prime and $e_{1}, e_{2}, \ldots, e_{k} \geqslant 1$. Then the positive divisors of $N$ are of form
$$p_{1}^{f_{1}} p_{2}^{f_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{f_{k}}$$
where $f_{i} \in\left\{0,1, \ldots, e_{i}\right\}$ for each $i$. That is, there are $e_{i}+1$ possibilities for $f_{i}$ for each $i$, and hence $N$ has
$$ \left(e_{1}+1\right)\left(e_{2}+1\right) \cdots\left(e_{k}+1\right) $$
positive divisors. Thus we need to find how to write 14 as a product of numbers of form $e_{i}+1$, where $e_{i} \geqslant 1$. There are two ways:
$$14=13+1 \text { or } 14=(1+1)(6+1),$$
since $14=2 \times 7$ (prime decomposition). Thus numbers of form $p_{1}^{13}$ or of form $p_{1}^{1} p_{2}^{6}$ have 14 positive divisors, where $p_{1}, p_{2}$ are different primes, and the least positive integers of each form are $2^{13}$ and $2^{6} \cdot 3$, respectively.
Since, $2^{6} \cdot 3<2^{13}, N=2^{6} \cdot 3=64 \cdot 3=192$.

Solution. Answer: 162. For convenience, let the sides of the smaller squares be $a, x, b$, respectively, so that $a^{2}=72, x^{2}=A, b^{2}=98$. Firstly,
$$ \begin{aligned} a^{2} & =72=6^{2} \cdot 2 \\ \therefore a & =6 \sqrt{2} \\ b^{2} & =98=7^{2} \cdot 2 \\ \therefore b & =7 \sqrt{2} \end{aligned} $$
So,
$$ \begin{aligned} 318 & =a x+a b+b x \\ & =x(a+b)+a b \\ \therefore x & =\frac{318-a b}{a+b} \\ & =\frac{318-6 \sqrt{2} \cdot 7 \sqrt{2}}{6 \sqrt{2}+7 \sqrt{2}} \\ & =\frac{318-84}{13 \sqrt{2}} \\ & =\frac{234}{13 \sqrt{2}} \\ & =9 \sqrt{2} \\ A=x^{2} & =81 \cdot 2 \\ & =162 \end{aligned} $$

wajo25_q12.solution:
Solution. Answer: 701. Let $a, b, c$ be the side lengths of Amy's, Ben's, and Cass's cubes, respectively. We have
$$ \begin{aligned} 204 & =12(a+b+c) & & \\ 630 & =6\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right) & & \\ a & =2 b & & \\ 17 & =3 b+c, & & \text { substituting }(3) \text { in } \frac{1}{12}(1) \\ 105 & =5 b^{2}+c^{2}, & & \text { substituting }(3) \text { in } \frac{1}{6}(2) \\ & =5 b^{2}+(17-3 b)^{2}, & & \text { substituting for } c, \text { using }(4) \\ & =14 b^{2}-102 b+289 & & \\ \therefore 0 & =14 b^{2}-102 b+184 & & \\ 0 & =7 b^{2}-51 b+92 & & \\ & =(7 b-23)(b-4) & & \text { since } b \in \mathbb{Z} \Longrightarrow b \neq \frac{23}{7} \\ \therefore b & =4, & & \text { by }(3) \\ a & =8, & & \text { by }(4) \\ c & =17-3 \cdot 4, & & \\ & =5 & & \\ \therefore V & =a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3} \\ & =8^{3}+4^{3}+5^{3} \\ & =512+64+125 \\ & =701 \end{aligned} $$
Therefore, the total volume of the three cubes is 701.

wajo25_q13.solution:
Solution. Answer: 300. For convenience let the distance Alan and Bob run be 1 unit, and let the speeds that Alan and Bob run be $a$ and $b$ (in units per min.), respectively. Then, noting that the time in minutes that Bob took to run the whole distance is $1 / b$,
$$ \begin{aligned} 3 a+3 b & =1, \quad \begin{array}{l} \text { since between them Alan and Bob } \\ \text { cover the whole track in } 3 \text { min. } \end{array} \\ \therefore 3 a & =1-3 b \\ \frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b} & =\frac{5}{2} \text { min. } \\ \therefore \frac{1}{a} & =\frac{1}{b}+\frac{5}{2} \\ \therefore \frac{2 b}{a} & =2+5 b \end{aligned} $$
$\therefore(1) \cdot(2): 6 b=(1-3 b)(2+5 b)$
$$ \begin{aligned} & =2-b-15 b^{2} \\ \therefore 0 & =15 b^{2}+7 b-2 \\ & =(5 b-1)(3 b+2) \\ \therefore \frac{1}{b} & =5 \text { min., since } \frac{1}{b}>0, \text { and hence } \frac{1}{b} \neq-\frac{3}{2} \\ & =300 \mathrm{~s} \end{aligned} $$
So Bob took 300 seconds to cover the distance.

wajo25_q14.solution:
Solution. Answer: 26. Since $M N$ is a midline of $\triangle A B C$, and $P=\operatorname{midpt}(B C)$,
$$M N \| P C \text { and } P C=\frac{1}{2} B C=M N$$
$\therefore M N C P$ is a parallelogram
$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore O & =\operatorname{midpt}(M C)=\operatorname{midpt}(N P) \\ K & =A O \cap M N, \text { where } A O, M N \text { are medians of } \triangle A M C \\ \therefore K & =\operatorname{centroid}(A M C) \\ \therefore K N & =\frac{1}{3} M N \\ & =\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{2} B C \\ & =\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 156 \\ & =26 . \end{aligned} $$

wajo25_q15.solution:
Solution. Answer: 39. This is a discrete optimisation problem. Essentially, we will deduce $\min (k)=B$, for some integer $B$, by showing:
(i) $k \geqslant B$, ( $B$ is a lower bound for $k$ ), and
(ii) $k=B$ is attainable via an example.

Consider 2 cases.
Case 1: $k \leqslant 38$. Then choosing $k$ even numbers, all sums are even and larger than 2, and hence not prime, contrary to the required condition. Therefore, $k \geqslant 39$.
Case 2: $k=39$. Partition $A$ into 38 pairs: $\{1,2\},\{3,76\},\{4,75\}, \ldots,\{39,40\}$. (There are 38, since the first numbers of the pairs are all the numbers from 1 to 39, except for 2.) Observe that each pair sums to 3 or 79 (prime), so that if we choose 39 numbers from $A$, then by the Pigeon Hole Principle, necessarily both numbers of one of the listed pairs must be chosen, guaranteeing that a pair of numbers whose sum is prime is chosen.
So from Case 1., we have $k \geqslant 39$, and by Case 2., $k=39$ is attainable.
Hence $\min (k)=39$.
